questions.q: Why not just hash every file and drop exact copies?
questions.a: A hash only matches byte-identical files. A copy with a renamed variable or a changed licence header slips through. In The Stack, after exact copies were already removed, near-duplicate detection still found 38.6% of the files in its permissive-licence set.

In Allamanis's 2019 study, the Java-Large dataset split by project still had 8.9% of its test set duplicated in training, against an expected 24.1% with a random 60/40 split by file. Forks and pasted-in libraries cross repositories, so group by fork network and by near-duplicate cluster too.

questions.q: A time-based split makes the test harder. How do you tell that apart from leakage?
questions.a: Our reasoning: re-run the previous model on the same new split. A harder test lowers both models' scores. Leakage mostly shows up as the new model's lead shrinking, because the copies it had memorised are no longer in the test.

questions.q: Why does a random split by file leak on GitHub data?
questions.a: GitHub is full of copies; the DéjàVu study found 70% of files in 4.5 million non-fork projects were clones. A random split by file puts copies on both sides, so many test files have a twin in training.

questions.q: Name three kinds of group to keep on one side of a code split.
questions.a: Whole repositories, fork networks (a repo, its forks and their forks), and clusters of near-duplicate files found with a method such as MinHash. Or split by date instead.

teach.title: How it works: checking a code split

questions.q: How do you find out whether a big jump came from leakage?
questions.a: Count test files with an exact or near copy in training. Re-split by group or by date, re-run both models, and compare. If the new model's lead shrinks on the clean split, leakage explains that part of the jump.
